newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-AUSTRALIAN GENERAL NEWS - AUG 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-AUSTRALIAN GENERAL NEWS - AUG 7.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Cigarette company WD & HO Wills (Australia) last night suspended sales of its products and requested a 48-hour suspension of trading in its shares. The action is in response to the High Court's decision to abolish State taxes on petrol, alcohol and tobacco. age 1.

Outlays by retail investors into equity funds have quadrupled over the last financial year and reached their highest recorded level. Approximately A$1.8 billion was invested in equity funds in the 12 months to June 30. Page 1.

BHP's sweeping review of its global operations reaped its first corporate victim yesterday with the resignation of BHP Minerals executive general manager Dick Carter. The announcement of his departure coincided with confirmation of increased cost overrun and start-up delays to BHP's hot briquette iron plant near Port Hedland in WA.

The National Australia Bank's monthly business survey has found that business conditions deteriorated in July. The NAB says the survey has reinforced its opinion that significant economic growth is unlikely to occur during the 1997-98 year. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

The Federal Government has established a special policy unit to combat negative images of Australia generated by Independent MP Pauline Hanson. The unit will focus on the Asian press and news wire services to ensure the Government's official position on ssues such as immigration and Aboriginal affairs is made public. Page 1.

Doubt has been cast on the viability of the Federal Government's A$6.5 billion tax rescue package for the States. Victoria, Western Australia and South Australia have all warned that price rises may be unavoidable and tobacco giant Wills has suspended sales of its products. Page 1.

Two British nurses accused of murdering Australian nurse Yvonne Gilford in Saudi Arabia, have launched legal action in South Australia designed to prevent their possible execution. The South Australian Supreme Court will hear an application on Friday whih seeks to overturn calls by the dead woman's brother, Frank Gilford, for the death penalty to be applied if the accused are found guilty. Page 1.

The owner of the Carrinya ski lodge destroyed in the Thredbo landslide yesterday declared he had a "clear conscience" and said the building had been approved by the National Parks and Wildlife Service. Richard Gallimore has further emphasised that the bulding was built according to all applicable regulations. Page 2.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

The Carinya and Bimbadeen ski lodges which collapsed in the Thredbo landslide were not subject to any conditions of approval by Snowy Mountains Shire Council. Documents uncovered yesterday reveal the lodges were built in the late 1960s and early 1970s when it was not yet decided what body was responsible for approving construction in the Kosciuszko National Park. Page 1.

Australia Youth Foundation chair Brian Burdekin warned yesterday that unemployed young people were being cheated of an essential rite of passage between adolescence and adulthood. Burdekin said the problem could not be solved by traditional methods such s structural adjustments and new industry policies designed to create job growth. Page 1.

New South Wales Premier Bob Carr acknowledged yesterday that a goods and services tax could be acceptable to the Australian Labor Party if accompanied by comprehensive guarantees of safety nets. The concession came as Federal Treasurer Peter Costello conirmed he wants major reforms to the indirect tax system following the High Court's decision to abolish State excises on tobacco, alcohol and petrol. Page 1.

A 23-year-old woman yesterday became the third self-confessed killer to be acquitted of either murder or manslaughter charges by a New South Wales Supreme Court jury in the past week. Belinda Lee Lowe was found to have acted in self defence when she killd an intruder in her home. Page 1.
THE AGE

The Victorian Government has shut down another two suburban train lines and reiterated its threat to close the entire train system as the dispute with transport unions deteriorates. The transport chaos coincides with disruption in the State's public hosptal system with nurses voting yesterday to close 20 per cent of beds and operating theatre sessions in response to a dispute over pay and staffing. Page A1.

Prime Minister John Howard is expected to return to work next Monday after an absence of three weeks due to pneumonia. Mr Howard will face a heavy workload as he is scheduled to chair a one-and-a-half day meeting of Cabinet on Monday then fly to Queenslad for speaking engagements that are part of a mid-term marginal seat campaign. Page A1.

The Australian Anglican and Lutheran churches have began discussions on an historic clergy sharing agreement. The agreement would allow their clergy to conduct services for people from either church. Page A2.

Newly appointed Australian Vice-Chancellors Committee president Professor John Niland vowed yesterday to campaign for improved higher education funding. Niland the vice-chancellor of the University of New South Wales, was elected earlier this week. Page 2.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
